canberra.title: Hanson accuses PM and Treasuer of inciting violence against her
canberra.snippet: Pauline Hanson has accused Anthony Albanese of inciting violence towards her by saying she and her One Nation party are divisive and dang...
canberra.content:
Pauline Hanson campaigning in WA for the Secret Harbour byelection last week. The One Nation leader says the Prime Minister and Treasurer have ‘crossed a line’. Photo: Pauline Hanson.

Pauline Hanson has accused Anthony Albanese of inciting violence towards her by saying she and her One Nation party are divisive and dangerous.

The Prime Minister delivered a strong rebuke of One Nation on Sunday (30 August) when addressing the party faithful at the Queensland State Labor Conference.

The day before, One Nation had snatched a seat from Labor to claim victory in a Western Australian state byelection.

“We have a Liberal Party that isn’t liberal, a National Party that isn’t national, and One Nation, whose leader seeks to divide Australians; talks Australia down both here and overseas,” Mr Albanese told conference delegates.

Later in his speech, the PM went further, describing Australia and the labour movement as at a crucial time.

“Across the world hard right populists are on the march,” he said.

“Peddling politics that is dangerous, divisive, and downright dishonest.

“We simply must defeat them. We owe it to history. And we will defeat them … They’ll say anything and do anything to win votes. Bend any facts. Peddle misinformation and disinformation. Turn Australian against Australian.

“Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to our problems.”

At the same conference, Treasurer Jim Chalmers also described One Nation as a “dangerous threat” to Australia.

“The threat to our country and its cohesion, its people, and our economy is posed by a dangerous and divisive coalition of chaos – a three-ring circus of Liberals, Nationals, and One Nation,” Dr Chalmers said.

“Today the biggest fault lines in our politics aren’t just between the centre-left and the extreme right, but between those of us who want to address and alleviate the legitimate frustrations that people feel about the cost of living and other pressures, and those who just want to picket them and prey on them, to politicise them and capitalise on them, while leaving our major challenges largely undisturbed.”

On Monday, Senator Hanson said the Prime Minister and his Treasurer Jim Chalmers had “crossed a line” in the way they had described her and One Nation.

She said such emotive language can incite political violence, as it did in the United Kingdom with the murder in July of former British conservative MP Ann Widdecombe.

The One Nation leader posted a lengthy social media post to denounce the pair and their speeches.

“The attacks from Chalmers and Albanese on One Nation have become increasingly desperate. Yesterday they crossed a line,” she wrote.

“No matter how worried Jim and Albanese are about losing their jobs, telling Australians that their democratically elected opponents are ‘dangerous’ and a ‘threat to our country’ invites people to treat them as a threat.

“Words have consequences. That is how political violence is incited.

“The murder of Ann Widdecombe in Britain should be warning enough about the dangers of poisonous political rhetoric.

“Anthony Albanese says we need to turn down the heat and violent rhetoric in our political discourse.

“Meanwhile, he and his Treasurer are pouring petrol all over it.”

Senator Hanson said Australians are entitled to vote for One Nation without being told by the Treasurer and the Prime Minister that their democratic choice is a danger to the nation.

“The real danger is that Jim and Albanese’s incompetent economic management will continue to push your rent, your mortgage and your bills even higher,” she said.

“The real danger to Jim and Albanese is that the people of Australia are coming for their government … at the ballot box.”

The One Nation leader subsequently posted that she supported free speech and open debate as “fundamental parts of our democracy”, but drew the line at “normalising and encouraging” potential incitements to violence.

“Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese crossed that line yesterday in their attacks on One Nation,” she said.

“Free speech and open debate is only possible when everyone is protected from the threat of violence in response to what they say.

“Labor politicians seem to get a free pass to use language they would never allow others to use.

“When democratically elected parties are described as ‘threats’ and a ‘danger to the country’ by the Prime Minister and the Treasurer, people will take those words seriously.

“Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese need to take their own advice and ‘turn the temperature down’.”

One Nation’s win in the WA state electorate of Secret Harbour is the first the party has secured in that state’s Lower House and shows it is not only a threat to the Coalition but also to Labor.

Federal Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie holds the seat of Canning, which encompasses the state electorate One Nation has just won.

canberra.title: Drink ‘spiker’ sentenced for role in violent ordeal that left woman with 44 injuries
canberra.snippet: After having her drink ‘spiked’, a woman was trapped in a car and violently assaulted for two hours before she managed to esc...
canberra.content:
Casey-Lee Pricsina, 35, has been sentenced by the ACT Supreme Court. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

After having her drink ‘spiked’, a woman was trapped in a car and violently assaulted for two hours before she managed to escape.

One member of the trio behind the incident, Raymond Kevin Ziebell, was handed six-and-a-half years’ jail over his role last year before it was Casey-Lee Pricsina’s turn to be sentenced by the ACT Supreme Court.

The female victim met Ziebell and Pricsina, who had been in a relationship at the time, through a mutual contact before they went to her home in December 2023 to repair her fence.

Pricsina returned to the woman’s home late the next night and asked to come inside before they shared a drink. The woman left her drink unattended on occasion that evening, and on her return, thought it tasted weird, like medicine.

Ziebell also arrived before Priscina convinced the woman to go with them to a McDonald’s.

They got into Ziebell’s car, and he drove off before the woman realised there was a third person inside the vehicle, the then-35-year-old Kristie Lee Watson of Scullin.

For the next two hours, the trio trapped the woman inside the car, accused her of taking drugs or money and threatened to cut her up and get to her daughter before one, alleged to be Watson, demanded $10,000.

Acting Justice Louise Taylor, in her recently-published decision, said Watson repeatedly punched the woman in the face and also repeatedly hit her in the face with a metal bat, dislodging one of her teeth.

When Ziebell finally pulled over, he threatened to cut the woman up with an electric saw before burying her where they stopped.

He also strangled her until she couldn’t breathe, put his knee in her chest and punched her in the face.

Raymond Kevin Ziebell (left) tries to hide his face from media after leaving court. Photo: Albert McKnight.

The woman managed to get out of the car and started running, but Ziebell and Watson chased her and tripped her up. She again managed to escape and ran to the Molongolo Water Quality Control Centre in Holt, near Shepherds Lookout.

She was taken to hospital with 44 different injuries over her body.

“Since then, my life has narrowed to a corridor of fear and isolation,” the woman went on to tell the court.

“I rarely leave the house and find shopping malls unbearable. At night, I have to lock my daughter and myself in our room to find some sense of safety to fall asleep.”

Pricsina pleaded guilty to recklessly inflicting grievous bodily harm and forcible confinement, both by joint commission.

Acting Justice Taylor said she was jointly criminally liable for everything inside the car until it stopped, when Ziebell and Watson went beyond the agreement they had made with her.

The acting justice said Pricsina hadn’t inflicted the violence herself that night, but she lied to the woman to engender her sympathy and to encourage her trust and also “spiked” her drink in an effort to facilitate the offending.

“This deception was critical to the victim’s eventual willingness to leave the safety of her residence and voluntarily enter the vehicle,” the judge said.

Acting Justice Taylor did say Ziebell had exerted a level of manipulation and control over Pricsina in their relationship, which influenced her in becoming involved in the offences.

Pricsina had a disadvantaged childhood and began using drugs when she was 14. She is now aged 35, is unemployed and said she had received Centrelink payments for about 15 years.

She was sentenced to about three years and one month’s jail with a one-year and five-month non-parole period, which means she can be released from custody in December 2027.

Watson died in August 2025.

canberra.title: Wagga Council issues $110 fine to homeless pensioner at Wilks Park
canberra.snippet: Housing advocates have condemned Wagga Wagga City Council for issuing a $110 fine to a disabled pensioner living in a bus at Wilks Park. ...
canberra.content:
31 August 2026

Start the conversation

A fine Wagga Council issued to a pensioner on Monday. Photos: Supplied.

Housing advocates have condemned Wagga Wagga City Council for issuing a $110 fine to a disabled pensioner living in a bus at Wilks Park.

The man was among at least three people fined by council compliance officers on Monday (31 August) after refusing to leave the park.

Council compliance officers and NSW Police had previously visited Wilks Park on 11 August, issuing dozens of letters telling people they had to vacate the site by Tuesday, August 25, or risk being fined.

Many rough sleepers at the park had been offered what the NSW Government calls “temporary accommodation” – essentially hotels and motels.

But with every hotel room in Wagga booked out on 25 August, council officers did not undertake any compliance action that day.

At least three people were issued fines on Monday, including the disabled pensioner living in the bus.

The fines were issued for failing to comply with the “terms of a notice erected by council”.

Housing advocates noted that the police and compliance officers had been respectful and courteous, but the issuing of penalty notices was distressing for people who had nowhere else to go.

“I really don’t know what they are supposed to do; they don’t have the money to pay the fines,” Tim Verhoef said.

He said moving into a hotel was not the answer because people did not want to give up all their possessions to move into a small room temporarily.

Wagga Council defended its actions in a statement released on Monday.

“Council staff and NSW support agency staff are attending Wilks Park from today as part of a three-day compliance operation to address ongoing breaches of the site’s conditions of stay,” a spokesperson said.

“Throughout the operation, council staff will continue to encourage anyone sleeping or residing in temporary structures at the site to take up the accommodation and support services being offered. Homes NSW and Vinnies have continued to actively engage with people living at Wilks Park and other identified homelessness encampments, offering accommodation and support to assist with relocation.

“Most individuals have actively engaged with support services and accepted accommodation options. Council has provided additional time for people to make arrangements before commencing formal compliance action and has offered temporary storage facilities to assist those transitioning into housing.”

Police and compliance officers at Wilks Park on Monday.

The council said it would not fine people who engaged with support services.

“However, several people staying at Wilks Park have consistently declined offers of accommodation and support. Compliance action will now be undertaken where individuals continue to stay at the site in breach of the conditions of stay.”

Wagga councillor Richard Foley said fines were not the answer.

“It’s a pointless exercise to issue fines to people who don’t have the capacity to pay,” he said.

“But while council are looking like the bogeyman, it’s the NSW Government who are at fault. I offered them a positive solution to this crisis immediately after a baby died in the tent, but they have ignored us.”

In May, Cr Foley sent Housing Minister Rose Jackson a submission outlining a pilot proposal to establish a modular tiny-home village supported by wraparound services to address the homelessness crisis.

He said he had not even received an acknowledgment of his submission.

Wagga Council said it would also continue to clean up former campsites and restore Wilks Park to its intended use for the wider community.

“Wilks Park is a primitive campground that provides basic facilities and permits stays of up to 72 hours,” a spokesperson said.

Kira Levin, principal solicitor of the Homeless Persons’ Legal Service at the Justice and Equity Centre, said anyone who received a council fine should seek legal advice from her organisation or Legal Aid NSW.

She also said fines were the wrong approach.

“Enforcement like this doesn’t work; you’re moving the problem somewhere else or forcing people into hiding, which puts them more at risk,” Ms Levin said.

“It’s disappointing that they’ve got to the point where council is fining people.”

Ms Levin said the problem was that there was no long-term plan for people experiencing homelessness.

“People know their only option is to move into a hotel or hide.”

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: New map reveals how the new light rail corridor will be greened
canberra.snippet: More than 140 large trees will adorn the light rail route from Alinga Street to Commonwealth Park in a major planting program to green an...
canberra.content:
31 August 2026

Join the conversation

3

Commonwealth Avenue where rows of Himalayan Cedar and Chinese Elm have already been planted. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

More than 140 large trees will adorn the light rail route from Alinga Street to Commonwealth Park in a major planting program to green and soften the impacts of the $577 million project.

Canberrans can now discover where and what species have and will be planted with the publication of a new interactive map on the Built for CBR website.

The Light Rail Stage 2A Tree Plantings Map provides an interactive guide to the city’s planned urban tree canopy, including the locations of new trees, the species selected, and the environmental benefits they will provide.

The new plantings feature a mix of deciduous and evergreen species that will complement existing trees along London Circuit and Commonwealth Avenue, including Himalayan Cedars (Cedrus deodara) and Pin Oaks (Quercus palustris).

Other species to be planted are London Plane, Chinese Elm “Yarralumla”, Zelkova Green Vase or Japanese Elm, Weeping Myall, Tulip Tree and Red Spotted Gum.

Infrastructure Canberra said the trees were already growing at Yarralumla Nursery, so trees could be well advanced before being planted as part of the project. Many were standing over four metres tall.

It said the Himalayan Cedars planted along Commonwealth Avenue had been propagated from the same seedstock source as the trees south of the lake near Albert Hall planted under the direction of Charles Weston.

The more than 100-year-old Himalayan Cedars in the Commonwealth Avenue median are slated to be removed when the planned Light Rail Stage 2B to Woden alignment is constructed through the Parliamentary Zone.

On the Northbourne Avenue median between the Sydney and Melbourne Buildings, green tracks will be flanked by plantings of deciduous Green Vase Zelkova.

Along London Circuit, deciduous, climate-resistant London Plane trees will dominate. These trees were selected on the advice of the National Capital Design Review Panel to maintain a consistent streetscape and provide symmetry with the numerous other London Plane trees across the city.

The interactive map says Commonwealth Avenue’s tree selections strengthen its historic character as an elegant tree-lined boulevard.

Along the verges, there will be rows of evergreen Himalayan Cedar and deciduous Chinese Elm, while between the green tracks in the median will be a row of Pin Oaks well suited to the Canberra climate.

Small strategic stands of Tulip Trees and Red Spotted Gum round out the selections.

Infrastructure Canberra said that, once established, the new trees along Stage 2A were expected to increase tree canopy coverage along the route to more than 30 per cent, in line with the targets of the ACT Government’s Urban Forest Strategy 2021-2045.

Infrastructure Canberra said planting had already commenced on parts of the alignment, with new trees in position outside the Sydney and Melbourne Buildings, and on the Commonwealth Avenue verges.

Further planting is scheduled for later stages of the construction program.

canberra.title: Warmer winter plants seeds for a ‘cocktail’ of pollen this spring
canberra.snippet: It’s looking like it’ll be a rough start for hay fever sufferers this spring, but relief could be on the horizon. That’...
canberra.content:
31 August 2026

Start the conversation

Dr Simon Haberle is in charge of the Canberra Pollen Monitoring Centre – and he says this spring could bring a “cocktail” of pollens. Photo: James Coleman.

It’s looking like it’ll be a rough start for hay fever sufferers this spring, but relief could be on the horizon.

That’s the message from Professor Simon Haberle, director of the Canberra Pollen Monitoring Centre at the Australian National University (ANU).

He says a “cocktail” of different pollens is on the cards this spring.

When asked what it means for hay fever sufferers, Professor Haberle says it depends on the climate.

“There’s good and bad in this scenario,” he tells Region.

“This coming season – because it’s forecast as being an El Niño period – we anticipate that the grass pollen in particular will be average or below average.

“That’s good news for Canberrans … there could be quite a bit of variability.”

Professor Haberle says there could be an early peak to the circulation of grass pollens this spring.

“This year there’s a forecast for El Niño, which I think will not only bring warmer temperatures but much drier periods as well.

“We anticipate that the grass growth period will probably be stronger (early on) but the grass will die off fairly early – potentially it will reduce the impact of grass-related hay fever.”

That could mean life gets easier for hay fever sufferers and asthmatics as the year goes on.

“What we are anticipating, given the warmer temperatures … [is] that there’ll be a strong burst of grass pollen that usually starts in that last week of September to early October,” he says.

“That’s the pollen that most people suffer hay fever symptoms from.

“That could be a bit early, but we’re waiting to see what the data tells.”

Ryegrass is among the plants releasing pollen as the weather warms – and it can blow “from many tens of kilometres away into the city”. Photo: Damien Larkins.

The bush capital is also affected by “a lot” of tree pollen, including cypress pine, birch, casuarina and “a whole range of other tree types”.

Most trees will start to flower in the coming weeks, though some, like pinus and cypress pine, have already begun (you can thank them for the yellow dust on your car over the past few days).

Professor Haberle says that their pollen production is expected to continue until summertime arrives.

“Even though we’ve got a drier period, the tree can continue to produce a high degree of tree pollen,” he says.

“Unlike the grass, they don’t tend to dry off … [They’ll release] quite regular and large amounts of pollen. They’re less impacted by La Niña and El Niño, relatively, than the grasses.”

Professor Haberle predicts there will be an “average or perhaps below average risk” of Canberra recording ‘extreme’ pollen amounts this spring.

“The worst days – the most extreme pollen days – are when we have strong northwestly or westerly winds coming into Canberra.

“That’s when we see these big extreme days when people start to suffer and feel the effects of hay fever.”

Canberra Pollen posts information to its Twitter/X page on daily pollen counts and forecasts for Canberra.

australia.title: Queensland has set tough new rules around ebikes and e-scooters. What do they mean for riders?
australia.snippet: Transport minister says laws target ‘young hooligans’ holding ‘communities to ransom’, but cycling advocates say changes most affect law-...
australia.content:
This week, Queensland became the first Australian state – and one of the first jurisdictions on the planet – to set age limits and licensing requirements for e-vehicle riders.

Bicycle Queensland, the advocacy body for cycling in the state, says only a handful of other other jurisdictions around the world have passed similar legislation for ebike or e-scooter riders, such as New Jersey and Israel.

But how does the new legislation work, and what could other cities, states and countries learn from Queensland’s example?

One Nation has claimed victory in the Western Australian seat of Secret Harbour, delivering a massive blow to a safe Labor stronghold. With voter frustration over cost-of-living issues boiling over, what does this mean for the major parties heading into the next elections? australia.title: ‘Scary’: how misinformation and AI hallucinations are infiltrating Australia’s parliament
australia.snippet: Exclusive : Guardian analysis reveals that dozens of policy submissions from across the political spectrum incorrectly summarise real res...
australia.content:
Australia’s government inquiry process is supposed to help parliament make better decisions, hearing from experts and constituents alike. But Guardian Australia can reveal that the system is being flooded with AI-generated material, which is inventing studies and attributing nonexistent research to real academics and authors.

In some cases, committee reports have cited submissions in which the majority of sources appear to be AI-generated “hallucinations”, when large language models (LLMs) invent content that looks real but doesn’t actually exist.

If the phenomenon continues, there is a significant risk of parliamentarians “making decisions based on evidence that doesn’t exist”, says Christian Downie, a professor in the Australian National University’s school of regulation and global governance.

The situation is made more confusing by AI services including Google search. Previously, looking up an invented reference might produce results that would indicate the reference did not exist. Now Google’s AI summary will sometimes create summaries of a fake reference as though it were genuine.

In some instances, Google’s AI summary and ChatGPT will also cite the inquiry submission with the fake reference as a source, creating an ongoing cycle of misinformation.

One document submitted to an inquiry into family violence and suicide included a hallucinated reference attributed to Divna Haslam, a University of Queensland associate professor and clinical psychologist, and misstated her team’s research findings.

Haslam, who researches child and family adversity and maltreatment, says the reference was “scary” because it looked so real that someone taking a cursory look could be convinced. Google’s AI summary summarised the reference as if it were a real paper.

“It’s very frustrating to … to have invested time, money, effort, expertise in rigorous research,” she says. “Then to see something that’s inaccurate and inappropriately attributed anyway is really concerning.”

The author of the submission, Drilldown Reports, told Guardian Australia it used AI in its research process and had identified the errors in its follow-up submission – but the deadline had passed to have them corrected.

“We do strongly believe in the human factor and that it should be a vital part of the full quality review process,” a spokesperson said. “Unfortunately, the human factor also lets us down when uploading the correct document.

“I get that you feel you have a juicy article to add the AI fear machine but this was a human error, not AI.”

The chair of the standing committee on social policy and legal affairs, which oversaw the inquiry, said all committees received a range of materials of varying quality and positions: “It is the job of the committee to both accept the evidence offered on face value but then also interrogate it through the inquiry process.”

Haslam says not only does this phenomenon risk devaluing legitimate research but there are serious risks if misleading information makes its way into government policy. “Particularly in a [domestic violence] space,” she says. “We just can’t risk that.”

Dozens of submissions contained errors

The paper was just one of dozens the Guardian identified by building a computer program that extracted references from all inquiry submissions made to the current parliament and checked those references against several online academic databases.

Documents that were flagged as having a high proportion of references not matching anything were then manually checked.

Using these methods, the Guardian found at least 39 submissions to political inquiries containing what appear to be hallucinated references.

These findings represent a conservative estimate of the amount of AI-generated material in political processes, as it only identifies submissions with incorrect citations. This approach would not find documents that used AI to generate text without any references, for example.

In another indication of how often LLMs are being used, more than 100 papers included ChatGPT url tags in reference links, which are automatically added by the platform in its results.

The submissions containing AI-generated material range from documents with a small number of incorrect citations to submissions in which every reference cited does not exist. They were authored by individuals and organisations across the political spectrum.

When Guardian Australia contacted the people and organisations responsible, many were unaware AI could get things wrong in this way or were aware of the potential for errors but had missed them before submitting the document.

How governments will grapple with AI-generated errors in material intended to influence policy, or whether they have the tools and resources to identify them, is an emerging question. Last year the consultancy giant Deloitte issued a partial refund to the federal government after it was revealed that AI tools had included fake references and even a fake court reference in a $440,000 report.

Downie says if public documents like government submissions or even court judgments are found to contain fake material or fake citations, the implications could go beyond bad decisions.

“We’re also starting to undermine the public’s trust and confidence in the types of institutions that underpin our democracy,” he says.

‘A first draft, not a final source’

While misleading claims or invented citations are not a new problem, greater access to LLMs has allowed this to grow at unprecedented levels.

One submission to a housing inequity inquiry this year included what appears to be references to work by Nicole Gurran, an academic at the University of Sydney, that does not exist.

Transparency and contestability are a vital part of the research and peer-review process, which is why citations are used as evidence to back up claims, says Gurran, a professor of urban and regional planning.

“Fake citations, even if an accidental ‘collage’ where the claim is correct but the chain of reference to evidence is broken, undermines that,” she says.

Another paper submitted last year to a Senate inquiry into climate change misinformation by the National Rational Energy Network said the Guardian was “left-leaning, activist-oriented” – and appeared to attribute that claim in part to an “article” by Margaret Simons, a journalist and academic, in a top journal.

But Simons – who is on the board of the Guardian’s owner, the Scott Trust – never wrote such a paper.

The endnote so accurately replicated other references that Simons briefly wondered whether it really existed. “Even though I know I didn’t write this, I did have that moment of self questioning,” she says.

NREN did not respond to a request for comment.

Senate advice for inquiry submissions warns that use of AI can present risks to the quality of information and that accuracy is the responsibility of the submitter.

Downie says the inquiry process needs to remain as open as possible but new guidelines may be needed to “encourage truthfulness”.

“Whether it’s climate change, immigration, health, we want our elected officials to be making decisions based on real information and real evidence not on fake citations and fake claims,” he says.

Guardian Australia asked OpenAI and Google how the companies were working to combat their role in the spread of misinformation.

OpenAI said addressing hallucinations was an ongoing area of research and that users should “use ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source”, ensuring that they verified quotes, data or references to external documents.

A Google spokesperson said AI Overviews operated “like traditional Search” in that they aimed to match content from the web to the words in the query: “AI Overviews – like traditional blue link results – will find and surface the web pages that include those terms.”

australia.title: Joe is used to the uncertainty of running a small business. But since Covid, ‘the whole world has changed’
australia.snippet: Australia is in the middle of a tidal wave of insolvencies as firms fail to cope with a ‘cost-of-doing-business crisis’ Get our breaking ...
australia.content:
Joe Rechichi, the CEO at Cucina hospitality group, has been in business for four decades, but says nothing compares to what he has experienced over the past few years, not least because of the immense day-to-day uncertainty.

“I call it BC and AC – Before Covid and After Covid,” says Rechichi, who oversees three Andiamo Trattoria restaurant venues across Sydney’s inner west.

“Whether it’s the cost of compliance, the cost of utilities, the whole world has changed and it’s not clear what it takes now to be a successful business.”

Rechichi says his business is increasingly at the mercy of conditions that are largely beyond his control – and often from overseas – such as war in the Middle East, cost-of-living pressures and the fallout from the pandemic.

“I used to pride myself on my budgets. Before Covid, you just knew where you were going and could make decisions about your business. Since Covid it has been the worst trading conditions.”

Surging wages, rents and electricity bills are hitting profit margins across corporate Australia. At the same time, firms are struggling to grow their revenue amid entrenched consumer pessimism in an economy stuck in low gear.

The compliance burden grows heavier every year, business owners say, and upcoming rule changes, from credit card surcharges to the plans to hike tax on trusts, threaten further costs and uncertainty.

Australia is in the middle of a tidal wave of insolvencies, as firms struggle and increasingly fail to cope with what could be described as a cost-of-doing-business crisis.

Just as households grapple with how to make the family budget stretch for another month, firms are also wondering if they will be able to keep their heads above water from one quarter to the next, let alone from year to year.

Many thousands are submerging; the number of companies entering into insolvencies has surged over the past two years to reach record levels.

Innes Willox, the chief executive of the Australian Industry Group, says that there are about 70% more insolvencies a year now than there were going into the pandemic period.

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

Firms managed to survive through the Covid lockdowns thanks to extraordinary levels of taxpayer-funded support, alongside forbearance by the Australian Taxation Office when it came to enforcing tax debts.

As a result, the number of companies becoming insolvent plunged through 2019-20 and 2020-21 to average about 4,600 across the two years, according to Asic data.

Unsurprisingly, as support rolled off the number of business failures returned to pre-Covid levels of about 8,000 a year in 2022-23. But then they jumped past 11,000 in 2023-24 – the most in data stretching back to the turn of the century.

Analysts interpreted this surge as a form of “payback” as the firms who may have failed earlier were it not for Covid support were now hitting the wall.

Except, as Willox notes, “the number of insolvencies didn’t normalise as we would have expected”.

Business failures climbed again to reach nearly 15,000 in 2024-25, or 40% above the last peak of about 10,800 in the early to mid-2010s. In the most recent financial year they were barely lower at 14,150.

“We are in phase two: businesses that have come out of Covid got through that first wave of insolvencies, and are now falling by the wayside,” Willox says.

Helen Owens, the founder and owner of Brisbane’s Tigerlamb hair salons, has experienced plenty of ups and downs in the 21 years since she started her business – not least the global financial crisis and then the “tears and pain” of Covid.

But right now feels different, Owens says.

“Pressure is coming from everywhere and all at once.”

Owens feels like her four salons have navigated their way through the worst of the times, and is proud of that – even as she recognises many business owners are not in the same position.

“I know everybody right now is treading water.”

She has seen so many businesses dying that she says “it feels like an episode of the Squid Game”, referring to the TV series about a dystopian survival gameshow.

While the raw insolvency numbers look dramatic, the picture is less dire when assessed relative to the number of firms, as the Reserve Bank of Australia has noted.

By this measure, insolvencies as a share of operating businesses was 0.5% in the most recent financial year, or about 1 in 200.

But that is still a long way above the 0.36% rate in 2018-19 and substantially higher than the pre-pandemic average of about 0.4%.

Willox believes the country is experiencing “a period of structurally elevated business insolvencies”.

The combination of weak demand and high and rising costs is particularly threatening for small businesses, which typically operate at much tighter margins than the bigger end of town.

Research by the RBA in April 2025 found that small firms accounted for more than eight in 10 insolvencies over the preceding few years.

Nearly nine in 10 small businesses say the cost of doing business is higher than a year before, according to a recent survey of small regional firms by the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia (Cosboa).

Three-quarters also told the survey their profits were down on a year earlier.

Skye Cappuccio, Cosboa’s chief executive, said that was the second year in a row where her members were reporting rising costs and falling profits.

Meanwhile, CreditorWatch, a commercial credit agency, recently reported that one in eight cafes and restaurants had closed in the past year.

Patrick Coghlan, CreditorWatch’s CEO, said the statistics included businesses that did not become insolvent but decided to pull up stumps and cancel their business registrations.

CreditorWatch data on business-to-business payments shows high rates of firms not paying suppliers on time or defaulting on their payments – a warning sign of more business failures to come.

But business owners are natural optimists, and Owens says she does not feel like today’s business climate is the “new normal”.

“Currently there is not that feeling that we are coming out the other side for most business owners, but I’m excited because I know it will happen.”

As for Rechichi, he says while his customers are coming out less often, when they do, they’re making a bigger night of it.

“I’ve got a better handle on what I need to do in the business, so dollars are starting to trickle down to the bottom line.”

world.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
world.snippet: Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks Airlink insist flyby conducted according to regulations A pre-game stunt involving ...
world.content:
A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of around 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks.

The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

Flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41 to 46 feet (12 to 14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.

Airlink, a sponsor of the South African rugby union team, said that the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft travelling at around 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over another stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But this weekend’s flyby was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” said Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said on Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.

Airlink said that the flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed that their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

world.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
world.snippet: Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination A UN committee has said countries...
world.content:
A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.

The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.

“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.

At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.

Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.

Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.

Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

world.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration Spain’s prime minister,...
world.content:
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.

“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday. “Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”

Sánchez said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.

The accusation drew a furious response from Israel. The country’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, called it a “brazen lie”, adding: “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not distract from Sánchez’s disgraceful failure to manage his country’s affairs.”

The ⁠Kremlin rejected allegations ⁠that ​Russia was connected to ⁠the Ceuta migration crisis, the ⁠RBC daily ​reported ‌on ‌Monday.

Sánchez repeated his assertion that the influx was due to the activities of “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.

Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, at least 1,500 people, including minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta. Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.

Sánchez said there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.

Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.

world.title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city
world.snippet: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts Humanitarian conditions...
world.content:
Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.

The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.

“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.

The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”

The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.

“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”

Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.

Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.

Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.

A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.

The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.

Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”

Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.

Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”

So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.

With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.

Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.

“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”

Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”

Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

world.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
world.snippet: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours Austrian police are hunting...
world.content:
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.

The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”

Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.

MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.

Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.

The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.

A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.

European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.

In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.

This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.

A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.
